lessons.title: The legal framework and workforce planning
lessons.html:
HR management in agriculture

Labour is often a farm's largest controllable cost and its greatest source of productivity and risk. Human resource management (HRM) covers planning the workforce, recruiting and selecting, contracts and conditions, training, performance, employee relations and compliance.

Key labour legislation

LawMain focus
Basic Conditions of Employment Act 75 of 1997Working hours, overtime, leave, notice, payslips, records; supplemented for farm workers by the sectoral determination for the agricultural sector
National Minimum Wage Act 9 of 2018Minimum wage levels, including those applying to farm workers
Labour Relations Act 66 of 1995Freedom of association, collective bargaining, unfair dismissal and unfair labour practices, CCMA dispute resolution
Employment Equity Act 55 of 1998Prohibits unfair discrimination; affirmative action duties for designated employers
Skills Development Act 97 of 1998Workplace skills planning, learnerships, SETAs (AgriSETA for agriculture)
Occupational Health and Safety Act 85 of 1993Safe workplaces
Compensation for Occupational Injuries and Diseases Act 130 of 1993Compensation for work injuries and diseases
Unemployment Insurance Act 63 of 2001UIF benefits and registration of workers

Minimum wage levels and specific conditions are updated by notice; always check the current values rather than relying on old figures. Farms that provide housing must also be aware of tenure security legislation affecting occupiers.

Workforce planning

  1. Determine labour requirements from the farm plan: tasks, hours and skills per month for each enterprise.
  2. Compare with the current workforce: numbers, skills, age profile, expected resignations and retirements.
  3. Plan to close gaps with permanent staff, seasonal workers, labour brokers or contractors, mechanisation or training.
  4. Plan for peak seasons such as harvest and packing well in advance, including transport, accommodation and supervision.

Job analysis

Job descriptions set out purpose, duties, reporting line, required skills and working conditions. Job specifications set out the qualifications and experience needed. They form the basis for recruitment, grading, pay and performance management.

lessons.title: Recruitment, performance and employee relations
lessons.html:
Recruitment and selection

  • Advertise through channels that reach suitable candidates: local notice boards, community structures, agricultural colleges, online platforms. Avoid criteria that unfairly discriminate.
  • Shortlist against the job specification.
  • Use structured interviews with the same questions for all candidates, plus practical tests for skills such as tractor driving or pruning.
  • Check references and verify qualifications and licences.
  • Issue a written contract stating job title, pay, hours, leave, deductions, notice and any probation period, and induct the new worker on safety, rules and procedures.

Training and development

Use a workplace skills plan to identify training needs, prioritise them and source accredited training, for example through AgriSETA-supported learnerships. Training records support compliance, grading and promotion.

Performance management

  1. Agree clear standards and targets linked to the job description.
  2. Monitor performance and give regular feedback.
  3. Hold formal reviews, recognising good performance and agreeing improvement plans where needed.
  4. Link incentives to measurable outputs where appropriate, such as quality-adjusted picking rates, while ensuring minimum wage compliance.

Poor performance (incapacity) is handled differently from misconduct: it requires guidance, training, a reasonable time to improve and fair procedure before dismissal is considered.

Discipline and grievances

A written disciplinary code and grievance procedure should be explained to all workers. Discipline must be fair both in substance (a valid reason, a known rule, consistent application, appropriate sanction) and in procedure (notice of allegations, an opportunity to respond, representation as the code allows, a decision and right of appeal). Corrective, progressive discipline such as counselling and written warnings is preferred for less serious offences. Disputes about dismissal may be referred to the CCMA.

Employee relations and wellbeing

Regular communication through worker committees, respect for freedom of association, fair treatment, decent housing and sanitation, and attention to health issues such as HIV, TB and substance abuse build trust and reduce turnover and conflict.

Key points

  • Know the main labour laws: BCEA, National Minimum Wage Act, LRA, EEA, SDA, OHS Act, COIDA, UIF.
  • Plan the workforce from the farm plan, including seasonal peaks.
  • Recruit with structured, fair, job-related selection and written contracts.
  • Manage performance with clear standards, feedback and fair incapacity procedures.
  • Apply discipline that is substantively and procedurally fair.
